card.stem: A living room has a solid concrete ground floor with a 20 mm quarry tile finish as shown. The external wall of the living room is a 350 mm concrete block wall with an insulated cavity. The wall is plastered on both sides. The foundation is a traditional strip foundation.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the external wall and ground floor. The section should show all the construction details from the bottom of the foundation to 400 mm above finished floor level. Indicate the typical sizes of four main components.

rows.verbatim: Any 7 of the above details (5 marks each)
rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: 19 mm render and 13 mm plaster; 100 mm outer leaf; DPC; 50 mm residual cavity; wall tie; 100 mm insulation; 100 mm inner leaf; 120 × 20 mm skirting; 20 mm quarry tiles sealed at the wall; 150 mm concrete floor; 150 mm floor insulation; DPM or radon barrier; hardcore and sand blinding; concrete fill or foundation blocks; reinforced concrete foundation.
Typical sizes of four main components, 1 each.

rows.verbatim: Draughting, accuracy and scale (excellent, good, fair)
rows.contextNote: Draughting, accuracy and scale of the section, excellent, good or fair, up to 8.

card.stem: The owner of a house built in the 1960s intends to improve the thermal insulation levels by insulating the external walls and the attic space. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with an uninsulated cavity. The attic space is also uninsulated. It is proposed to inject insulation into the cavity of the external walls.
card.questionText: Using notes and neat freehand sketches, describe the procedures to be followed when injecting the insulation into the cavity. Specify the type of insulation to be used.

rows.contextNote: Such as: carried out by a specialist company registered with SEAI; 22 mm holes drilled through the outer leaf at 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically, with extra holes at cills and heads.
A second, different step. Such as: polystyrene beads pumped in with a light glue that sets them solid; the holes filled and blended with the external finish.
Such as: polystyrene beads.
A valid detail on the sketch, as in the scheme’s model sketches.
Quality of the sketch, excellent, good or fair, up to 5.

card.questionText: List two specific safety precautions to be observed in each of the following situations and give one reason for each safety precaution listed: using a ladder when painting an external wall; using a veneering knife to cut veneers; using a jig saw to cut a wooden panel.

rows.verbatim: Safety precautions using a ladder when painting an external wall
rows.contextNote: Two precautions 5 each and reasons 4. Such as: a ladder in good condition on firm level ground at 1:4; no over-reaching, three points of contact; coned off from traffic and held by a helper — the angle and over-reaching are dangerous.

rows.verbatim: Safety precautions when using a veneering knife to cut veneers
rows.contextNote: Two precautions 5 each and reasons 4. Such as: a sharp, good-quality knife on a solid surface; a straight edge held firmly to guide it; light passes; concentration — a sharp knife on a firm surface is safer.

rows.verbatim: Safety precautions when using a jig saw to cut a wooden panel
rows.contextNote: Two precautions 5 each and reasons 4. Such as: the wood firmly clamped; the lead clear of the blade; cut slowly; eye and face protection and a mask — moving wood and a cut lead are dangerous.

sourceMaterial.label: ORIGINAL QUESTION 6
sourceMaterial.title: Ladder, veneering knife, jig saw and outdoor tool safety

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and neat freehand sketches, any five of the following: concrete lintel; mortice and tenon; energy rating; door saddle; quarter sawing; ridge board; triple glazing; window cill; vapour barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Concrete lintel: a reinforced, often pre-stressed, concrete beam spanning the opening over a window or door, carrying the blockwork above to the wall on either side; its length suits the opening. Mortice and tenon joint: used in furniture, doors and windows: a mortice formed in one piece and a tenon, ideally a third of the thickness, on the other to fit it. Energy rating: the BER of a dwelling, an A to G rating of its energy performance and CO₂ emissions, compulsory when a house is sold or rented since 1 January 2009. Door saddle: a hardwood or softwood piece, typically 110 × 15 mm, fixed at the bottom of the door frame, giving clearance under the door and covering the joint between floor coverings. Quarter sawing: radial conversion of a log cut parallel to the rays, giving stable boards that wear evenly and silver grain in oak; expensive and labour intensive. Ridge board: the horizontal softwood member at the apex between the tops of the rafters, giving the roof rigidity and straightness; opposite rafters are nailed to it. Triple glazing: three layers of glass giving better insulation, sound performance and U-value, less condensation and a comfortable temperature, ideal on exposed sites. Window cill: usually a reinforced concrete unit under the window, sloping away to shed rainwater, with a drip beneath; also PVC, stone, steel or wood. Vapour barrier: a continuous membrane on the warm side of insulation slowing water vapour into it (the 5:1 rule); used in timber frame walls, flat roofs and attic conversions.
